The Consumer Price Index (CPI) and the GDP deflator move together most of the time, but there are clear exceptions. In 1979 and 1980, the increase in the CPI was significantly larger than the increase in the GDP deflator. This discrepancy arises because the CPI measures the price of goods consumed in the United States, while the GDP deflator measures the price of goods produced in the United States. When the price of imported goods increases relative to the price of goods produced in the United States, the CPI increases faster than the GDP deflator.

This process led to the creation of multiple layers of securities, making it difficult for banks to assess the value of the underlying mortgages.
